title: A Pilot Ejected Above a Thunderstorm. It Kept Him in the Air for 40 Minutes
description:
Case 007, the full case file. On 26 July 1959 Lt. Col. William Rankin of the U.S. Marine Corps, a veteran of the Second World War and Korea with about a hundred combat missions, led a pair of F-8 Crusader jets from South Weymouth, Massachusetts, toward Beaufort, South Carolina, with Lt. Herbert Nolan on his wing. To clear a thunderhead topping out around 45,000 feet they climbed to 47,000 feet (about 14 km), flying just under the speed of sound. Rankin heard a thump and a grinding from his engine, the fire warning light came on and the engine stopped. The emergency power handle broke off in his hand. He radioed that he had a power failure and might have to eject, and at about 6 p.m. he did, with a helmet and an oxygen mask but no pressure suit, into air around 50 below zero. The blast tore off his left glove and that hand went numb; decompression swelled his abdomen. He got his mask on and breathed his emergency oxygen, waiting for a parachute set to open by itself at 10,000 feet, a free fall of about three and a half minutes. It opened early, inside the storm; most accounts say the storm's air pressure tripped the automatic release. Updrafts and downdrafts then threw him up and down, by his own account as much as 6,000 feet at a time, through hail he feared would tear the canopy, lightning he described as blue blades several feet thick, thunder he felt rather than heard, and rain so dense that he breathed in water. The canopy collapsed and draped over him before filling again. About forty minutes after ejecting he came out under the cloud over North Carolina, was swung into the trees, hit a trunk head first with his helmet on, and read 6:40 on his watch. He walked to a country road, where about a dozen cars passed him; Time magazine reported that one finally slowed after a small boy inside said there was a jet pilot standing in the road. He was taken to a country store, lay on the floor until an ambulance came, and was treated in hospital at Ahoskie, North Carolina, and then at the naval hospital at Beaufort for frostbite, welts and bruises and decompression shock. He spent weeks in hospital, returned to flying, told the story in his 1960 book The Man Who Rode the Thunder, retired from the Marine Corps in 1964 and died on 6 July 2009. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. Scenes, sets and all of Rook's actions are dramatised; nobody's words are quoted directly.

source_notes: LONG-FORM ADDITIONS (checked on 14 Nov 2026). How it was checked: seven pages were opened for this run and read for these facts: Time magazine, 'Heroes: The Nightmare Fall', 17 Aug 1959 (the contemporaneous report, which quotes Rankin; 'Time' below); Wikipedia (William Rankin; it rests mainly on Gavin Pretor-Pinney's The Cloudspotter's Guide and cites Time and Rankin's book); White Eagle Aerospace ('Riding the Thunder', J. Terry White, 26 Jul 2020; 'WE'); We Are The Mighty (Ward Carroll, 2021, with block quotes from Rankin's memoir; 'WATM'); Damn Interesting ('Rider on the Storm', Alan Bellows, Oct 2011; 'DI'; the article body was read in full, the reader comments were not used); Task & Purpose (James Clark, 17 Jun 2016, which relays Time's quotes; 'T&P'); and Chapelboro / WCHL ('Local Lore', Victor Lewis, 15 Mar 2019). Rankin's book itself was not read. T&P and Chapelboro largely repeat Time and Wikipedia, so they are treated as secondary checks, not independent ones. Who: Lt. Col. William Henry Rankin, U.S.M.C. (all). War record: 'a hundred battle missions and a bail-out in enemy fire over Korea' (Time); 'more than 100 combat missions during World War II and the Korean War' (T&P); veteran of both wars (Wikipedia, WATM, DI, Chapelboro). The script says 'about a hundred combat missions'; the tally in the record insert is a graphic, not a count. His age is not given: Time, DI and T&P say 39, but Wikipedia's birth date (16 Oct 1920) makes him 38 on the day. His squadron is not named in any page read and is not mentioned. The flight: 26 July 1959, a two-ship of F8U (F-8) Crusaders from South Weymouth, Massachusetts, to Beaufort, South Carolina (Wikipedia, WE, WATM; Time says the 'return leg of a high-altitude flight to Boston' to the 'Marine Auxiliary Air Station at Beaufort, S.C.'). DI's body text says Beaufort, North Carolina, which is an error against the other sources. Rankin led (WE: 'formation commander'); wingman Lt. Herbert Nolan (Time, WE, WATM, DI, T&P; WATM says 1st Lt., T&P says 'Navy Lt.', WE 'Marine Lieutenant'; the script says 'Lieutenant'). Take-off about 5 p.m. (WE only; not stated in the film, which shows a daylight take-off). The climb: thunderhead peaking at 45,000 ft (Wikipedia) or around 44,000 ft (WE); the script says 'around forty-five thousand'. Cruise at 47,000 ft (Time, Wikipedia, WATM, DI, Chapelboro; WE says they climbed to 48,000 and the engine seized at 47,000). Speed: Mach 0.82 (Wikipedia), 500 knots true air speed (Time), 'near the speed of sound' (DI), 'just below the speed of sound' (Chapelboro); the script says 'just under the speed of sound'. The failure: 'a loud bump and rumble' (Wikipedia), 'thump and grinding noises' then another thump (WE), 'a loud grinding noise' (WATM), 'a grating, rasping jolt' (Time); fire warning light (Wikipedia, WE, WATM); 'The engine stopped' (Wikipedia), 'His engine had seized' (WE). The handle: the auxiliary power lever 'broke off in his hand' (Wikipedia; WATM, Chapelboro similar); WE names it the ram air turbine handle; Time says only that he tried to coax power from an emergency generator. The script says 'emergency power handle'. Radio: 'Power failure. May have to eject.' is how Time (and DI, T&P after it) quote his call to Nolan; the script reports it indirectly ('He radios Nolan: power failure, he may have to eject') and the HUD label reads POWER FAILURE. What Nolan did afterwards is not in any page read; the wingman's jet 'holding station, then banking away' is dramatised. Equipment: no pressure suit (Wikipedia, WATM, DI, Chapelboro); 'jet helmet, oxygen mask and his parachute' (Time); 'a light summer flying suit' (WE). Ejection: 'He pulled two overhead handles' (Time), at about 6:00 p.m. (Wikipedia, WE '1800 hours EDT', DI 'approximately 6:00pm'). Cold and decompression: -50 C (Wikipedia), -65 F (Time, T&P), -70 F (WE), -58 F (Chapelboro); the script keeps 'around fifty below zero'. Left glove lost in the ejection, left hand numb (Time: 'My left hand went numb. I had lost that glove when I went out'; WATM, DI). Abdomen: 'I had a terrible feeling like my abdomen was bloated twice its size' (Time); the script reports this indirectly ('until, he said, it felt twice its size'). Bleeding from the eyes, ears, nose and mouth (Wikipedia, WE, T&P) is reported and is not shown or mentioned. Free fall: he got his oxygen mask on and used his emergency oxygen (WE, WATM, Wikipedia, DI). Parachute preset to open automatically at 10,000 ft, 'the safe-breathing level' (Time; also Wikipedia, WE, WATM, DI, T&P); expected free fall 'about three and a half minutes' (WATM, DI). Why it opened early: Time's footnote says the release height 'was considerably higher in Rankin's case, because of the barometric turbulence of the storm'; Wikipedia, DI and Chapelboro say the storm tripped the barometric switch; WE gives 15,000 to 20,000 ft and no cause; WATM alone says he thought the mechanism had failed and pulled it himself, while Time quotes him: 'Just as I was considering pulling the cord, I felt a shock.' The script says 'By most accounts, the storm's wild air pressure tripped the release early.' No opening height is given. Inside the storm: 'I was blown up and down as much as 6,000 feet at a time', 'like being on a very fast elevator' (Time); hail, 'I was afraid the hail would tear the chute' (Time; DI); lightning as blue blades or sheets 'several feet thick' (Wikipedia from The Cloudspotter's Guide; WATM; WE 'luminous sheets of blue'); 'I never exactly heard the thunder; I felt it' (Time); 'I'd take a breath and breathe in a mouthful of water' (Time); holding his breath (Wikipedia) and fear of drowning (WATM, DI, WE); the parachute 'draped over me like a sheet' and then blossomed again (Time; DI); 'At one point I got seasick and heaved' (Time; DI, Wikipedia, WE). All are reported indirectly. The up-and-down trace in the graph insert is an illustration, not his real track; the shock rings in the thunder shot are a visual figure. Duration: 40 minutes (Time, Wikipedia, WE, DI, T&P); watch 6:40 p.m. on landing (Wikipedia, DI, Chapelboro). WATM's memoir extract has him reading 'twenty minutes past six' while still in the air. Coming out: 'I figured I was down to 300 or 500 feet' (Time), 'just a few hundred feet from the ground' in 'a warm summer rain' (DI); the script says 'a few hundred feet above North Carolina'. Landing: 'Swept by stiff ground winds, his chute fouled in a tree, and Pilot Rankin slammed headfirst into the tree trunk' (Time; DI, T&P, Chapelboro; DI and Chapelboro credit the helmet). WATM's 'thicket of brush in the middle of a field' is not followed. The road: Time says he found 'a country road' and that 'A dozen cars passed him'; DI has him walking a search pattern to a back road; WATM 'a number of vehicles that refused to stop'. The script says 'About a dozen cars'. The boy: Time only: a car slowed after a small boy said there was a jet pilot standing in the road; the script attributes this to Time by name and the film shows a child at a car window; the car, the driver and the boy as drawn are invented in appearance. Store and ambulance: the car 'took him to a country store, where he collapsed on the floor while waiting for an ambulance' to 'a hospital in Ahoskie, N.C.' (Time; DI and T&P similar; DI places the store in Ahoskie and has him telephone himself, T&P says an ambulance was called). In the film a storekeeper is on the wall telephone; who made the call is dramatised. Hospital and after: Ahoskie, then 'the Beaufort Naval Hospital, where he is recovering from frostbite and shock' (Time); 'frostbite, welts, bruises, and severe decompression' (Wikipedia; WATM, DI similar; Time calls the injuries 'remarkably minor'); 'about 3 weeks in the hospital' (WATM), 'several weeks' (DI); the script says 'weeks'. Returned to flying (WE: 'returned to flying as a Marine aviator'; WATM 'returned to flight status'). The book: The Man Who Rode the Thunder, Prentice-Hall, 1960 (Wikipedia, WE; DI 'the following year'); the book in the film is our own drawing, not the real jacket. Service 1940 to 1964 (Wikipedia), retired 1964 (T&P). Died 6 July 2009 (Wikipedia, DI), in Oakdale, Pennsylvania (Wikipedia, T&P); DI: 'almost exactly 50 years after'; his age at death is 88 in Wikipedia and 89 in WE and WATM, so it is not given. Not used because only one page has it: the jet crashing about 20 miles away with nobody hurt and the 65 miles between ejection and landing (WE), the 70-minute planned flight (WE), the lightning flash that lit the canopy (Wikipedia). Dramatised in the long form, not reported: the look of every new set (the country store inside and out, the petrol pump, the hospital room, the study), the take-off as drawn, the cockpit action around the radio call and the handles, the tumbling and the moment the mask goes on, the collapsed canopy as drawn, the walk through the woods, the cars and the ambulance (no markings), the storekeeper, the driver, the doctor and his clipboard, the dressings on his hands, the typewriter, and everything Rook does. The Time card on the case board is our own card, not the magazine's page or logo. No dialogue is attributed to anyone; on-screen words are labels. FROM THE SHORT: Read for this run: Wikipedia (William Rankin; its account rests mainly on Gavin Pretor-Pinney's The Cloudspotter's Guide, 2006, and cites Time, 'The Nightmare Fall', 17 Aug 1959, and Rankin's own book), White Eagle Aerospace ('Riding the Thunder', J. Terry White, 2020), We Are The Mighty (Ward Carroll, 2021, quoting Rankin's memoir) and MiGFlug (2026; it follows the Wikipedia account closely, so it is treated as a secondary check, not an independent one). The Task & Purpose page could not be opened by this run and is not used; the Time article and the book were not read directly. Agreed by all: 26 July 1959; Lt. Col. William Rankin, U.S. Marine Corps; an F-8 (F8U) Crusader; South Weymouth, Massachusetts to Beaufort, South Carolina; engine failure and a fire warning light at about 47,000 ft (14.3 km), just above a thunderhead topping out around 44,000-45,000 ft; the auxiliary/emergency power handle (the ram-air turbine handle) broke off in his hand; he ejected at about 6 p.m.; no pressure suit (White Eagle says 'a light summer flying suit'); his abdomen swelled from decompression and he was frostbitten; the parachute opened inside the storm; updrafts carried him back up; lightning he described as blue sheets or blades several feet thick; rain so dense he held his breath for fear of drowning; he landed in North Carolina and recovered. Where the sources differ: (1) Temperature: -50 C (Wikipedia, MiGFlug) or -70 F, about -57 C (White Eagle); the script says 'fifty below zero' and the thermometer insert stops at -50 with no unit. (2) Why the parachute opened: Wikipedia, White Eagle and MiGFlug say the storm tripped the barometric release early (it was set for 10,000 ft; White Eagle says it opened between 15,000 and 20,000 ft); We Are The Mighty says he feared the release had failed and pulled it himself. The script says only that it 'opens inside the storm'. (3) Hail: Wikipedia, White Eagle and MiGFlug; We Are The Mighty does not mention it. (4) Duration: 40 minutes from ejection to landing, watch reading 6:40 p.m. (Wikipedia, MiGFlug; White Eagle '40 minutes' by his watch). 'It should take minutes': We Are The Mighty gives about three and a half minutes of free fall to 10,000 ft, MiGFlug says a normal descent should have lasted less than ten minutes; the script gives no figure. (5) Landing: 'a forest' (Wikipedia, White Eagle), 'through trees near Ahoskie' (MiGFlug), 'a thicket of brush in the middle of a field near Ahoskie' (We Are The Mighty); the script says 'into trees in North Carolina' and the film shows pine woods. (6) Help: he reached a dirt road where several vehicles passed before someone took him to hospital (We Are The Mighty); a passing driver took him to a country store to phone for an ambulance (MiGFlug); Wikipedia says he searched for help and was admitted to hospital at Ahoskie. The script says 'He walks to a road, gets a ride.' (7) Where the storm was: near Norfolk, Virginia (White Eagle) or over North Carolina (We Are The Mighty); not stated in the film. (8) The lost left glove appears in We Are The Mighty and MiGFlug only; the film shows one bare hand. Returned to flying: White Eagle and We Are The Mighty (about three weeks in hospital in the latter only, so no duration is given). Bleeding from the eyes, ears, nose and mouth is reported by the sources and is not shown. His wingman, Lt. Herbert Nolan (White Eagle, We Are The Mighty), appears only as the second jet and is not named. Dramatised, not reported: the look of the jet (no markings), cockpit, flight suit, helmet and parachute colours; the airfield; the exact motion of the fall; the hand to his mask in the rain; the car on the road; his waving it down; the closing shot of him beside a jet; the flight-chart case board (the coastline is a sketch, not a map); and everything Rook does (the stowaway seat, the small parachute, the pocket watch). No dialogue is attributed to anyone.
